title: The Day of the Lord Will Come
summary: Peter answers scoffers who say that Christ's promised coming will never arrive because nothing ever changes. God's word made the world and judged it by the flood, and by the same word the present world is kept for judgment. The Lord is not slow but patient, wanting all to repent, and his day will come suddenly. Believers should live holy lives as they wait for a new heaven and a new earth, guard against error, and grow in grace and knowledge.
story: Chapter 2 described the false teachers' character; chapter 3 answers their central argument. They mocked the promise of Christ's return, saying that the world goes on as it always has. Peter reminds his readers that he is writing a second letter to stir their memory, most likely pointing back to 1 Peter, and calls them to remember both the prophets and the command of the Lord given through the apostles. The chapter closes the letter by setting the whole Christian life between the promise and its fulfillment: waiting, living holy lives, and growing.
historical:
By the time this letter was written, the first generation of Christians was dying. Verse 4 has the scoffers say that the fathers have fallen asleep, a common Christian way of speaking of death; the fathers may be the first Christian leaders, or the patriarchs of Israel. Either way, the early expectation that Jesus might return soon had not been fulfilled on the timetable some had assumed, and critics used the delay to argue that there would be no return and no judgment. This is one reason many date the letter late in the first century, though defenders of Petrine authorship note that the problem could have arisen by the mid-60s, when Peter and others of the first generation were nearing death.

Verses 15-16 are historically striking. Peter calls Paul our beloved brother, refers to all his letters as if a collection were known to the readers, admits that some parts are hard to understand, and places them alongside the rest of the Scriptures. This is one of the earliest references we have to Paul's letters being read as Scripture, and it shows that his writings were already circulating and already being twisted by some.
cultural:
Many in the Greco-Roman world held that the universe was stable and eternal, or moved in endless cycles. Stoic philosophers taught that the cosmos would periodically be consumed by fire and then renewed, over and over. Peter's language of the heavens and earth reserved for fire has sometimes been compared with that idea, but his framework is different: a single, final day of judgment by the personal God who made the world, followed by a new creation where righteousness dwells. His picture comes from the Old Testament, which speaks of the Day of the LORD and of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22).

The elements of verses 10 and 12 (stoicheia) could mean the basic components of the physical world, as in Greek philosophy, or the heavenly bodies, the sun, moon, and stars, which ancient writers also called by this word. The image of the thief (verse 10) comes from Jesus' own teaching and was widely used in the early church for the unexpectedness of his coming.
literary: Peter builds the chapter as a reply. He quotes the scoffers directly (verse 4), then answers with four arguments. First, their claim that nothing changes ignores the flood, when God's word brought judgment on the world (verses 5-7). Second, God's time is not ours: a day is like a thousand years (verse 8), echoing Psalm 90:4. Third, the delay is patience, giving time for repentance (verse 9). Fourth, the day will come suddenly like a thief (verse 10). Then the chapter turns to exhortation, repeating the address beloved four times (verses 1, 8, 14, 17), and ends with a doxology to Christ. The repeated call to remember (verses 1-2) and to beware (verse 17) frames the whole.

outline.t: A reminder of the prophets and apostles
The scoffers and the answer from creation and flood
God's patience and the coming Day of the Lord
Holy lives while waiting for the new heaven and earth
Guard yourselves and grow in grace

doctrines.note: The Christian hope is not the survival of souls in a distant heaven but a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells (verse 13). The promise of Christ's coming gives shape and urgency to present life.
God's word that created the world also judged it at the flood, and it keeps the present order for a coming day of judgment. Delay is not denial.
God's patience has a purpose: he does not want anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (verse 9). The time between Christ's comings is a time of mercy.
Peter places the prophets and the apostles together as authorities, and he counts Paul's letters with the rest of the Scriptures, an early witness to the forming of the New Testament.

words.note: Parousia, presence or coming. In Greek it was used for the arrival of a ruler or official visiting a city. Christians took it up for the return of Christ in glory. The scoffers ask where the promise of his parousia is; Peter insists it is sure.

Makrothumeo, to be patient, literally to be long of temper. It describes the one who could act in anger but holds back. Peter uses it for God's delay: what looks like slowness is the patience of a God who wants people to repent.

Stoicheion, element or basic component. The word could mean the letters of the alphabet, the physical elements, the heavenly bodies, or the basic principles of a system. Here it probably refers to the building blocks of the cosmos or to the heavenly bodies, which melt or are destroyed in the fire of judgment.

christ: The chapter looks to the coming of Christ as the certain future of the world. Jesus is our Lord and Savior (verses 2 and 18), whose command was handed on through the apostles, and whose coming, like a thief, echoes his own words (Matthew 24:43). The letter's final sentence gives glory to Jesus Christ both now and to the day of eternity, an ascription of praise that the Bible elsewhere reserves for God, and so a quiet witness to his deity. The patience of verse 15 is the Lord's patience that brings salvation, the same patience the risen Christ extends before he returns as judge.

hard.q: Will the earth be burned up and destroyed, or renewed?
hard.a:
Verse 10 is notoriously hard, partly because of a textual question. Older translations followed later manuscripts that say the earth and its works will be burned up. Most modern translations follow early manuscripts that read something like will be found, which the BSB renders as “the earth and its works will be laid bare”. That reading suggests that the fire of judgment exposes everything to God's scrutiny rather than simply annihilating it.

Christians have taken two main views. Some read the passage as teaching the complete destruction of the present universe, replaced by a wholly new creation. Others read it as describing a purging fire that refines and renews the present creation, much as the flood (the comparison Peter himself makes in verse 6) judged the world without abolishing the earth. They point to Romans 8:19-23, where creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay. Both views agree on Peter's point: the present order is not permanent, everything will be judged, and God's promise is a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

questions: The scoffers argued that because nothing had changed, nothing would. Where do you see that same assumption in your own thinking about God and the future?
Peter says God's apparent slowness is patience that gives time for repentance. How does that change the way you read the delays and waiting in your own life?
Peter asks what kind of people we ought to be in light of the coming day. What would it look like for your hope of a new creation to shape an ordinary week?
